main_keyword: book about divorce for kids two homes
tagline: Two homes, two bedrooms, and the same love in both.
lesson_or_purpose: Helps a young child understand that parents living apart is a grown-up decision and not the child's fault, that some things stay the same in both homes, and that the child can take small steps to feel at home in each place.
tone: Gentle, honest and reassuring, with plain words and a calm, steady rhythm.
reading_level: Ages 3-8. Short sentences and simple, concrete words that a preschooler can follow when read aloud, with enough feeling and detail to hold an early reader. Light repetition of the phrase about things that stay the same.

illustration_guide: Soft, warm watercolor style with rounded shapes and gentle light. Two homes appear throughout: Mom's house in warm peach and butter yellow with a round window and a lemon tree by the door, and Dad's apartment in soft sky blue and sage green with a tall window and a balcony of potted herbs. The child's two bedrooms echo each colour scheme. Recurring elements on every page where it fits: a small plush fox that travels with the child, a striped travel backpack, a crescent moon visible through windows in both homes, and the child's crayon drawings that slowly fill both bedroom walls. Both parents look calm, kind and attentive, never angry. No words, letters, numbers or signs anywhere in the art.

h1: Personalized Two Homes Book About Divorce for Kids
meta_title: Personalized Two Homes Divorce Book | StoryBloom
meta_description: A personalized picture book for kids whose parents live apart: two homes, the things that stay the same, and it is not their fault.
promise: A gentle, honest story where your child learns that two homes can both feel like home, and that the grown-ups' decision was never their fault.
story_summary: When Mom and Dad explain that they will live in two homes, your child feels sad and mixed up, and quietly asks the question so many children wonder about. Both parents answer clearly that it is not their fault. At Dad's new apartment, the bedroom feels strange and bedtime is hard, until your child spots the same moon shining through the window that shines over Mom's house. That small discovery starts a search for all the things that stay the same.
why_parents: Young children often believe they caused big changes in their family, even when no one has said so. Hearing the words "this is not your fault" plainly, more than once, and seeing them said by both a mom and a dad character in a story, gives your child a clear message they can come back to again and again.

Moving between two homes brings real practical questions for a child: where will I sleep, what comes with me, what happens next. This story shows your child taking small, doable steps, like packing a comfort item, decorating a new room and using a picture calendar, so the change feels a little more understandable and a little more theirs.
for_grownups: After reading, ask your child: "What are some things that are the same at both homes?" Make your own list or drawings together, the way the child in the story does.
Children may ask "Is it my fault?" many times, sometimes long after the separation. Answering calmly and the same way each time is part of how the message sinks in.

If your child seems very worried, withdrawn or stuck in big feelings for a while, it can help to talk with your pediatrician or a family counselor. This book is a starting point for conversation, not a replacement for that support.

faqs.question: Does the book blame either parent?
faqs.answer: No. Mom and Dad are both shown as calm, loving and caring, and the separation is described simply as a grown-up decision. Neither parent is cast as the cause.

faqs.question: Is it suitable if my child is only three?
faqs.answer: Yes. The sentences are short and the ideas are concrete, like two bedrooms, a travel backpack and the same moon in both windows. Older children up to about eight can read along and talk about the feelings in more depth.

faqs.question: What if our family's arrangement is different from the story?
faqs.answer: The story keeps the details general: Mom has a house and Dad has an apartment, and the child moves between them on switching days. It works well as a conversation starter about your own family's schedule and homes, whatever they look like.

feed_description: A gentle personalized picture book for children ages 3 to 8 whose parents now live in two homes. Your child is the illustrated hero of the story. When Mom and Dad explain they will live apart, your child asks the question many children carry quietly, and both parents answer clearly that it is not their fault. At Dad's new apartment the bedroom feels strange at first, until your child notices the same moon shining over both homes and sets out to find all the things that stay the same. Along the way your child packs a favorite plush fox to travel between homes, fills bare walls with drawings and makes a picture calendar to know where they will sleep next. Warm watercolor art, plain honest words and a calm, reassuring ending.
